stories.title: Cracks emerge in AI borrowing boom as CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank debt worries grow
stories.summary: Another worry: the increasing number of data centres that are being delayed by permitting issues

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.title_zh: AI借贷热潮现裂痕：CoreWeave、Oracle与SoftBank债务担忧加剧
stories.content:
Another worry: the increasing number of data centres that are being delayed by permitting issues

TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom. But now there is growing uncertainty around just how easily more money can be obtained – and how much of it will be paid back.

Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave. Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.

Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.

At the same time, Wall Street investors have been bidding up the price of some complicated financial instruments that insure corporate debt against default, like those insuring SoftBank, the Japanese technology colossus that has borrowed heavily to bet its future on a partnership with OpenAI.

The recent market moves could spell losses for investors that own the companies’ existing bonds and could mean the companies will be forced to pay higher interest rates when they borrow again, raising the costs of their already wildly expensive AI projects.

The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.

The spread, or extra premium that investors demand to put their money into risky AI debt investments, has shot up more than 50 per cent over the past six months, according to Barclays, the investment bank.

“The market is on a knife’s edge everywhere,” said Alexandra Coleman, founder of Azraq, a data centre risk researcher.

A lot is riding on the continuation of the borrowing binge. Every week lately, economists, banks and private equity firms project higher and higher amounts of debt that they say will be needed to finance the AI systems that their boosters assert will run the world in a few years.

Virtually every major mutual fund company, insurer and private equity firm has been buying up the AI debt, to say nothing of the scores of individual investors who have poured money into skyrocketing AI companies.

Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally. The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals. Investors have also sold out of some these companies’ existing debt, though the drop in bond prices has been less steep than for CoreWeave.

CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description. Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.

First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips. Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more. CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.

Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future. Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.

A CoreWeave spokesperson, Lia Davis, said the company disagreed with the WeWork comparison. “The complexity of our financing reflects discipline, which is a point of pride for us,” she said in a statement.

Another worry is the growing number of US data-centre projects being delayed by permitting issues or, in some cases, falling through.

Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects. In 2025, the company easily borrowed US$38 billion from a group of banks to build, with the help of project developers, a pair of data centres, one in Texas and another on about 809 hectares of farmland in Port Washington, Wisconsin.

Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.

Since then, Project Lighthouse has run into local hurdles, including from state power regulators who have pushed back their time horizon to approve the construction of a power grid critical for the data centre to operate.

Aterio, a data centre researcher, said it was looking less likely that Project Lighthouse’s four data centres would start operating before 2029.

That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due. Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.

An Oracle spokesperson declined to comment.

Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico. The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.

Some of the US$18 billion in debt tied to the project has recently sold at steep discounts, roughly US$0.80 on the US dollar, according to two people familiar with the trades.

SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI. The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.

To get that money, Son sold off most of SoftBank’s holdings of Nvidia and T-Mobile and took out loans against his stake in chip designer Arm Holdings.

In 2026, Son invested again. On Oct 1, SoftBank completed another US$30 billion investment in OpenAI. Before doing so, in late September the company raised a record US$11 billion in debt at interest rates of nearly 10 per cent.

In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.

“The assets we’ve owned have increased significantly,” Clavel said in an interview.

The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked. It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt. At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.

Some investors see a potential silver lining to the troubles. John Lloyd, the global head of multisector and corporate credit at asset manager Janus Henderson, said slowing down the financing for projects “makes existing projects and existing AI infrastructure even more valuable.” NYTIMES

stories.title_zh: THMY扩产布局下一代AI芯片测试
stories.content:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 12, 2026 - October 18, 2026

THMY Holdings Bhd (KL:THMY), which made its ACE Market debut on Oct 23 last year at an initial public offering (IPO) price of 31 sen, has seen its shares surge nearly 7.5-fold in slightly less than a year to RM2.32 last Wednesday (Oct 7), giving the automated test solutions provider a market value of RM2.06 billion.

At that price, THMY trades at a trailing price-earnings ratio (PER) of about 123 times. Based on analyst forecasts, the stock is valued at 81 times the company’s earnings for the financial year ended March 31, 2027 (FY2027) and 59 times FY2028 earnings.

So, what is enabling the company to command such a lofty valuation?

The answer, according to CEO Ooi Can Nix, lies in THMY’s growing involvement in the development of increasingly complex products for the artificial intelligence (AI) and data centre industries. This includes working directly with a major US-based hyperscaler that designs its own specialised silicon chips.

“We are in their frontier products. Even \[for products that have not been launched\], we already work very closely with their design team,” Ooi tells The Edge.

Founded in 2008, THMY provides automated test solutions for electrical and electronic products, including in-circuit and functional circuit testing, as well as turnkey solutions covering design, fabrication, software development and assembly.

But its role is increasingly extending beyond simply supplying test equipment after a product has been developed. THMY is being brought into the development process earlier, working with customers to determine how their next-generation products should be tested and validating the engineering concepts before they enter commercial production.

“Before they come to the real product, we need to prove our design concept validation,” says Ooi. “We \[must\] have the solution, the engineering capabilities, the data to deploy into the complete test equipment system.”

This is becoming increasingly important as AI chips grow more powerful and generate significantly more heat. THMY can simulate a chip’s size, power requirements and heat generation, and work on solutions such as cold plates to manage the thermal load before the actual product reaches production.

THMY now has about 200 employees, including a sizeable pool of engineers, giving the company the technical capabilities to work alongside customers on increasingly sophisticated products.

For instance, THMY has developed modular systems that allow wear-and-tear components to be replaced more quickly, reducing downtime for customers. The need is becoming more pronounced as higher-power products put greater stress on testing equipment and accelerate component wear.

It is also benefiting from geopolitical shifts, particularly the China-plus-one strategy. Ooi says restrictions surrounding the development and deployment of certain data centre and AI products make Southeast Asia increasingly relevant as an alternative manufacturing and testing base.

“In Southeast Asia, not many companies are in this field. Compared to Western firms, we are better in terms of cost, in terms of efficiency. So that’s why we are in a pretty good position right now to grow,” he says.

As AI chips become more powerful, the infrastructure needed to test them is evolving just as quickly.

Ooi says earlier-generation products consumed less than 300W and could be tested using conventional air cooling. About two years ago, power requirements had risen to around 500W, making liquid cooling necessary. THMY is now working with products requiring about 1,500W, while the next generation could reach as much as 2,500W.

The jump in power density means THMY needs to invest not only in more sophisticated testing systems, but also in the power, cooling and other infrastructure needed to support them.

That rising infrastructure requirement is one reason THMY has substantially increased the scale of its second factory.

Initially planned at 88,000 sq ft, the facility has been expanded to about 300,800 sq ft, comprising 222,000 sq ft of factory space, 44,000 sq ft of office space and 34,000 sq ft of utilities.

The facility is designed to accommodate an initial 20 advanced automated test solution assembly lines, primarily for data centre and cloud computing AI products. Construction began in July and is targeted for completion by the second quarter of 2028.

The upsized project carries an estimated cost of about RM172.6 million, nearly six times the roughly RM30 million factory expansion outlined in THMY’s IPO prospectus.

More importantly, the facility is being designed with future product generations in mind, rather than simply to meet current demand.

“When we plan for the facility, we embed the upcoming requirements and long-term growth plans … as such, the floor space and infrastructure for high-capacity power supply,” says Ooi.

He expects the upgraded infrastructure to support at least the next five-year technology cycle.

The investment comes as THMY’s existing operations are already running at full capacity, despite the addition of mezzanine space and machinery.

Rather than turn away orders, however, the company is looking to stretch its capacity through automation, outsourcing, contract workers and Penang’s wider supply chain ecosystem.

“We won’t turn away our customers. In Penang, we’ve got a very strong ecosystem. We can utilise our networks, the supply chain system here, to help scale up \[business\],” says Ooi.

Automation is also helping THMY reduce its reliance on manual processes, with machines increasingly taking over inspection and other tasks that were previously performed manually.

THMY’s strategy is not simply to maximise production volume. Instead, it wants to use its engineering capabilities to capture more complex and higher-value projects.

Its technology, media and telecommunications segment — comprising data centre, AI-computing and telecommunications products — accounts for about 52% of group revenue, according to Ooi. Electrical and electronics and electronics manufacturing services contribute about 19% and 17% respectively.

Ooi says the group deliberately prioritises complex products because lower-value orders can consume substantial production capacity. “If we continue to focus on industrial products, consumer products, yes, the order is big, but the value is low,” he remarks. “That’s why we need to align \[business\] with our engineering competency and drive advancements on our capability. Then we can capture high-value products.”

That does not mean THMY is walking away from its legacy customers. Instead, it is increasingly outsourcing less complex processes and modularising assembly, allowing the group to preserve those relationships while freeing up internal capacity for more sophisticated work.

“For legacy products, we won’t turn down the customer. So, what we are doing is like in parallel, we outsource,” says Ooi. “For non-complex product assembly, we make it more modular and speed up the process.”

The strategy appears to be translating into higher margins. THMY’s net profit margin has risen steadily over the past five financial years, from 5.13% in FY2022 to 10.57% in FY2023, before rising to about 21% from FY2024 to FY2026.

The momentum has continued into FY2027. In 1QFY2027, revenue rose 42.5% year on year to a record RM20.2 million, while net profit more than doubled to a record RM6.2 million. Net profit margin widened further to a new high of 30.7%.

Ooi believes the shift towards higher-value projects should provide further room for margin expansion. “We look forward to the high-value projects and also selling our engineering competencies.”

While data centres and AI are the immediate growth drivers, THMY is already looking at the next technology wave.

Ooi identifies physical AI, particularly humanoid robots, as a potential new business segment.

THMY is already working with customers on new product introduction and conducting some testing on humanoid-robot components. Volumes are currently small, but Ooi sees potential for significant demand if humanoid robots move into commercial production.

“This is another area we are looking forward \[to\], how to expand our business sectors,” he says.

The group has historically positioned itself around successive technology cycles, having gained experience in consumer, industrial, networking and cloud computing products before the current AI boom. “We always keep ourselves in pace with the technology,” Ooi says.

The bigger factory will require funding beyond THMY’s remaining IPO proceeds.

As at June 30, 2026, the group had RM54.7 million in cash and bank balances, including other investments, with gearing at 0.35 times. It had RM28.78 million of IPO proceeds yet to be utilised, including RM22.9 million earmarked for the new factory.

Ooi says the remaining proceeds will not be sufficient for the projected capital expenditure. The company is working with several banks on financing facilities and is considering a combination of bank borrowings and equity funding.

THMY nevertheless remains mindful of maintaining a healthy balance sheet as it scales up, including the potential dilution from any equity fundraising.

“We are always mindful of the balance sheet and cash flow and not to stretch ourselves too much. We want to have healthy growth,” Ooi says.

On its market debut last year, THMY’s share price surged nearly three times from its IPO price to close at 91 sen. It then climbed a further 155% to its Oct 7 close of RM2.32.

Ooi says the management is keeping its focus on building the company’s technology capabilities and strengthening its operations, rather than on the share price.

“\[We are thankful\] to the capital market for believing in the company’s performance and the numbers we deliver,” he says. “For us, we are more looking forward to \[growing\] the technology-driven business.”

Affin Hwang Investment Bank, the sole research house with coverage of the stock, has a “buy” recommendation and RM3 target price. It forecasts THMY’s net profit to rise 88% from RM13.5 million in FY2026 to RM25.4 million in FY2027, before increasing another 36% to RM34.5 million in FY2028.

The target price is based on a PER of 83 times FY2027 earnings and 77 times FY2028 earnings.

For investors, the key question is whether THMY can deliver earnings growth fast enough to justify a valuation that has already moved far ahead of its IPO price.

As for Ooi, the focus is on staying ahead of the technology curve and preparing for the next generation of products.

Ooi remains THMY’s largest shareholder with a 67.2% stake, while the Employees Provident Fund and AIA Bhd hold 6.2% and 3.7% respectively.

stories.title_zh: 数据中心基础设施公司Elice上市首日暴跌33%，'惨淡首秀'重燃AI支出疑虑
stories.summary_zh: 首尔数据中心基础设施公司 Elice 上市首日下跌 33%，尽管其 IPO 募资 2,010 亿韩元，散户认购倍数高达 400 倍。疲软的上市表现重新引发了对 AI 基础设施支出热潮可持续性的质疑。

stories.content:
The Seoul-based firm’s IPO raised 201 billion won, with the retail tranche 400 times subscribed

\[SEOUL\] Shares of data centre infrastructure company Elice plunged in their trading debut, underscoring lingering concerns about whether the artificial intelligence boom can justify the billions of dollars being poured into the industry.

The Seoul-based neocloud service provider’s shares fell as much as 33 per cent in early trading, before paring the losses slightly.

That was an abrupt downturn after the company raised 201 billion won (US$151 million) in an initial public offering priced at the top of the marketed range, with the retail tranche 400 times subscribed.

The sell-off threatened to undermine a tentative recovery in Asian stocks, which had been buoyed by a rebound in US chipmakers as sentiment towards the AI investment boom improved.

Rather than reinforcing confidence, the quick plunge rekindled swirling concerns that have particularly impacted data centre companies, with some high-profile recent setbacks around the world.

Firmus Grid cancelled its Sydney IPO in October after investors balked at its valuation.

“It’s not a good sign, especially after Firmus pulled its IPO,” said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for Asia Pacific and Middle East at eToro. The “ugly debut” of Elice “hasn’t helped the dynamic in Asia today”.

Concerns over borrowing costs, fierce competition and long-term returns from massive AI-related spending have soured investor appetite for the sector.

Coreweave’s shares have more than halved since their May peak, AirTrunk is delaying a planned IPO of a real estate investment trust, people familiar with the matter have said, while Nscale is facing pushback over its target IPO valuation, Bloomberg News reported.

“Elice’s roughly 30 per cent drop at its IPO also hurts sentiment, signalling the environment surrounding neocloud companies has yet to fully improve,” said Kazuyuki Muramatsu, head of investment management at Nagomi Capital.

Founded in 2015 by three students in the doctorate program of Kaist, one of the country’s top technology universities, Elice began as a coding education platform before pivoting to AI cloud infrastructure, supplying products including servers, liquid-cooled chips, cloud and networking equipment and software.

The company has since developed a modular data centre platform with high-density power systems and advanced liquid cooling designed for high-performance AI chip clusters.

Elice sold its shares in the IPO at 90,500 won apiece, for a post-listing market capitalisation exceeding 1 trillion won. The shares sank to 61,000 won in early Tuesday (Oct 20) trading on the tech-heavy Kosdaq market, before rebounding to about 64,000 won.

## South Korea tightens scrutiny of new listings

The pressure on investor sentiment is against the backdrop of South Korea also weighing tighter scrutiny of new listings.

Authorities are examining whether a proposed US IPO of SK Hynix’s unit Solidigm would constitute a “duplicate listing”, a structure in which a company already owned by a plublicly traded parent lists its shares separately.

Critics argue that such deals can disavantage existing shareholders by allowing a subsidiary’s value to be unlocked separately. The debate adds another layer of uncertainty for companies seeking to tap public markets.

“Elice’s debut comes at a time when sentiment toward AI infrastructure companies has weakened, particularly in the US,” said Albert Yong, managing partner and chief investment officer at Petra Capital Management.

“Sentiment toward AI infrastructure has been highly volatile and often disconnected from underlying fundamentals.”

Elice was able to generate demand among South Korean retail investors, who poured roughly 10.3 trillion won into subscription deposits in hopes of buying shares.

But if the 33 per cent drop holds, it would become the worst-ever debut after a Korea IPO that raised at least US$100 million, surpassing the 30 per cent plunge by W-Scope Chungju Plant in 2022.

The stock’s plunge sent shockwaves across South Korea’s retail investment community, known as ants.

On Toss Securities’ popular mobile app, one poster shared an illustration of Alice – spelled similar to Elice in Korean – in Wonderland, smashing ants with a large hammer. “All ants are dying,” the post said above the illustration.

A user on X posted a screenshot of a 68,255 won position, down 24.75 per cent, on the day, saying: “This is the first time I’ve lost money on an IPO.”

Another investor wrote that the stock “ruined Korean stocks and crypto”, to which a comment said “I just want Elice to go away to Wonderland”.

“Retail investors may have blindly believed that IPO stocks would always go up,” said Jo Hyunik, an investment division manager at Seoul-based Iroom Investment Advisors.

To win over investors, Elice touted a 200 per cent surge in first-half revenue to 34.4 billion won, according to its prospectus.

The company swung to an operating profit of 10.3 billion won, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation jumped more than 11 times to 23.2 billion won.

The company is expected to record an 83 per cent sales jump in 2026 and an operating margin of about 33 per cent, analyst Douglas Kim wrote in a note on Smartkarma.

Elice’s financial structure is different from CoreWeave’s, and investors do not need to view the company as “particularly risky”, said Kim Dojoon, chief executive officer at Zian Investment Management. But, he added, “It remains to be seen whether the company can maintain its current profitability”.

A successful offering could have helped break an IPO drought in South Korea, where the primary market has been in the doldrums as fundraising surged across Asia.

First-time listings in Seoul have raised US$1.4 billion in 2026, compared with more than US$3 billion in each of the previous three years, according to Bloomberg-compiled data. Meanwhile, SK Hynix completed the biggest-ever US share sale by a foreign company.

Elice’s IPO was the biggest on the Kosdaq in 2026 and surpassed in Korea only by the US$337 million offering of K Bank in March.

Backed by venture capital firms including Vertex Ventures and Altos Ventures, Elice plans to use its IPO proceeds to build more AI data centres around South Korea and abroad, according to chief executive officer Jae Won-kim. Mirae Asset Securities and Samsung Securities served as lead underwriters.

“We’re going all-in on becoming a full-stack AI infrastructure leader globally,” Kim said in an interview. “This IPO is about giving ourselves the financial firepower to execute.” BLOOMBERG

stories.title: China Proposes AI Export Controls Affecting Open-Weight Models and Computing Clusters
stories.summary: China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology have proposed revisions to the technology export catalogue covering 23 AI-related technologies, including large models and computing clusters. The draft rules could restrict global developers' and Indian enterprises' access to Chinese open-weight models.
stories.why_it_matters: Export controls on open-weight models would extend the US-China tech decoupling into the open-source AI ecosystem, forcing overseas developers and enterprises to reassess reliance on Chinese foundation models.
companies: China Ministry of Science and Technology
stories.title_zh: 中国拟实施AI出口管制,影响open-weight模型与computing clusters
stories.summary_zh: 中国商务部与科技部提议修订技术出口目录，涵盖 23 项 AI 相关技术，包括大模型和算力集群。该草案可能限制全球开发者及印度企业获取中国 open-weight 模型。
stories.why_zh: 对 open-weight 模型的出口管制将把中美科技脱钩延伸至开源 AI 生态，迫使海外开发者与企业重新评估对中国基础模型的依赖。
stories.content:
China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology proposed revisions to the country's technology export catalogue.The draft rules cover 23 AI-related technologies, including advanced large models, AI agents, chip designs, and computing clusters. This proposal raises questions about the future availability of Chinese open-weight models outside the country, according to the Associated Press.For Indian businesses using models from Chinese companies such as DeepSeek and Alibaba, the controls could introduce uncertainty over future releases. They may also affect overseas deployment and commercial use.The proposed restrictions cover core AI models trained using important Chinese data. These models must meet computing requirements of 10-to-the-power-26 floating-point operations (FLOPs) or have two trillion parameters or more. They also include models ranking among the world's top 10 on relevant leaderboards, as reported by the South China Morning Post (SCMP).The draft also covers AI agents designed for sensitive environments, including national defence and critical information infrastructure. Chip designs and computing clusters are also included.China's Ministry of Commerce stated the controls are targeted and limited in scope. Access to certain AI services through application programming interfaces (APIs), websites, mobile applications, and software-as-a-service platforms would remain outside the proposed restrictions, Reuters reported. Most AI technologies would continue to be eligible for export.The public consultation on the draft runs until November 15, 2026. The final rules will determine which technologies require approval and how licensing requirements apply to overseas transfers.
### Impact on Open-Weight AI Ecosystem

Open-weight AI models make their trained parameters, or weights, available for others to download and run. Developers can use these models on their own infrastructure, fine-tune them, and integrate them into applications.Chinese developers have become important suppliers of open-weight models. DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen, and models from Moonshot AI and Z.ai are among the options for developers. The proposed controls could complicate overseas access to some of these models if transferring their weights from China requires regulatory approval.Alex Colville, an analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told the SCMP that new compliance requirements could delay or prevent Chinese AI companies from partnering with global cloud providers. This could affect the deployment of their most capable open-weight models overseas.A spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce told the SCMP that licensing for open-source AI technologies would be expedited with immediate clearance upon filing. However, Colville noted that the practical meaning of this process remained unclear.The proposed rules do not automatically mean developers must stop using Chinese models they have already downloaded. Developers Digest reported that weights already made publicly available would be exempt under the draft's provisions. Access through hosted APIs, websites, and applications would also remain outside the controls.This distinction matters for enterprises that have already integrated models such as DeepSeek or Qwen into their applications. The proposal does not, by itself, establish that these deployments must be discontinued.The position could be different for future models that meet the proposed thresholds. Overseas transfers of restricted technologies may require registration or licensing. Access to new model weights could therefore become subject to additional checks.

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 19): Peak electricity demand from the data centre industry in Peninsular Malaysia is projected to reach 8.39 gigawatts (GW) by 2030, based on the current electricity supply planning estimates, according to the Ministry of Energy Transition and Water Transformation (Petra).

Of the total amount, Johor is expected to record the highest demand for electricity at 4.42GW, and Selangor at 1.48GW.

“Both states are major hubs for data centre development and will therefore require proper electricity supply infrastructure planning that takes into account the anticipated growth in demand,” it said.

The ministry was responding to a question from Onn Abu Bakar (Pakatan Harapan-Batu Pahat) on the projected electricity and water demand by the data centre industry up to 2030, particularly in Johor and Selangor, as well as the number of data centres that have been completed.

Petra said 45 data centres had been completed and were operational in Peninsular Malaysia as of August, with a combined electricity supply capacity of 6.04GW.

This capacity refers to the electricity supply provided by Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA) through the national grid to support the operation of the data centres.

Meanwhile, the projected water demand from data centres in Selangor and Johor is expected to reach 389.04 million litres per day (MLD) by 2030.

“However, actual water consumption by data centres currently reported to the National Water Services Commission stands at 63.90 MLD,” Petra said.

stories.title_zh: CoreWeave的困境为何震动AI热潮
stories.content:
(Oct 19): CoreWeave's mounting debt is raising fresh concerns about the AI boom, as investors question whether demand can justify the billions being borrowed to build data centres.

Shares and bonds of the Nvidia-backed company have tumbled despite its CEO's assurances of a strong contract backlog, fueling a broader selloff in technology stocks.

Here is why investors are worried and what its troubles could mean for the industry.

CoreWeave rents out computing power from Nvidia processors to companies developing and running AI, including Microsoft and OpenAI.

It is one of the leading "neocloud" providers, a group of newer cloud companies that are growing rapidly to meet demand for scarce and expensive AI chips.

These neocloud companies give customers access to computing power without requiring them to build their own data centers. However, supplying such capacity requires heavy upfront investment in chips and infrastructure, often financed with debt.

The company, which has never turned a profit, has about US$50 billion in debt, according to data compiled by LSEG.

It raised its annual capital spending forecast by US$4 billion in August to between US$35 billion and US$39 billion. Analysts expect revenue of nearly US$13 billion this year and a loss of US$2.13 billion.

The yields on its bonds due in 2031, which are rated junk, have spiked to about 16%, while the cost of insuring its debt against default has climbed to about 1,000 basis points, reflecting growing concern among creditors.

CEO Mike Intrator told employees in an internal memo seen by *Reuters* that its deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations. The company had a US$104.2 billion revenue backlog at the end of the second quarter, followed by more than US$25 billion in new commitments early in the third quarter.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also downplayed the concerns, saying CoreWeave's financial strength is improving and he sees no need to backstop it. The chip giant has agreed to buy unsold CoreWeave capacity through April 2032.

the S&P 500 up four tenths and the Nasdaq rising more than one percent.

CoreWeave's business depends on two things: demand for AI computing and lenders' willingness to finance the infrastructure supplying it. But a selloff in its shares suggests a lack of confidence among investors in the latter, even as the company cites strong demand.

The concern is not that AI demand will collapse, but that higher borrowing costs could make the business harder to sustain if demand were to weaken sharply.

"It looks more like investors questioning how the build-out is being funded than a sudden collapse in appetite for AI computing," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group.

"CoreWeave is quickly becoming the AI trade's canary in the coal mine," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

Investors are questioning whether AI revenue can grow fast enough to cover the cost of building and financing the infrastructure.

CoreWeave has to spend heavily upfront before it can collect the revenue from its contracts. Higher interest rates could drive up financing costs and further squeeze returns.

The hardware itself poses another risk. Chips lose value as newer generations arrive, pushing providers to spend even more to replace them.

The concerns, however, go beyond CoreWeave. US technology giants are expected to spend more than US$700 billion on AI infrastructure this year.

One potential consequence would be a broader financing squeeze, with lenders demanding higher returns or becoming less willing to fund other AI projects.

That could force providers to scale back expansion, curbing equipment purchases and affecting the computing capacity customers expect.

A setback could also deepen doubts that the AI investment frenzy is outpacing returns, piling further pressure on technology stocks.

The impact of the fallout would depend on how the business is reorganized, and CoreWeave's ties to major technology companies do not, by themselves, mean its failure would trigger a wider financial crisis.

Gartner estimates about 80% of neoclouds could shut down by 2030, warning that expected AI revenue will not support profitable returns on all planned infrastructure spending.

Neocloud rivals Nebius, Applied Digital and Iren have fallen in the recent selloff. The cost of default protection has risen for SoftBank, which is betting heavily on OpenAI.

Meanwhile, spreads for Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia have also reached records, although they have risen much more slowly than CoreWeave's. However, these companies also have larger cash flows and stronger balance sheets.

stories.title: Small but mighty: micro data centres as the foundation of security and disaster recovery
stories.summary: Resilience-minded organisations are turning to compact edge systems to keep critical services running if cyberattacks, outages or floods hit.
stories.title_zh: 小而强大：微型数据中心成为安全与灾难恢复的基石
stories.content:
Tue, 20th Oct 2026 (Today)
Digital services now underpin almost every aspect of modern society. Banks process millions of transactions every minute, insurers rely on their IT systems to manage policies and claims, while governments deliver essential public services online. Any disruption to business continuity can have serious economic, social and reputational consequences, so as digital dependency increases, resilience must extend beyond cybersecurity software to include the physical infrastructure that supports these systems.

### A safety first approach

While hyperscale facilities and large colocation campuses continue to expand to support cloud adoption, artificial intelligence (AI) and data intensive applications, organisations are also recognising that not every workload belongs in a centralised data centre. The growth of edge computing, distributed applications and the requirement for faster, more resilient digital services is driving demand for smaller and highly available infrastructure platforms.

A key part of this evolution is the micro data centre. Typically housed within one standard 19-inch rack, they include power protection, cooling, fire suppression, security, access control and remote management in a compact format. Supporting critical loads starting from 3kW and going up to 100-150kW and providing enough power for localised computing without the overhead of larger facilities, micro data centres are redefining how businesses deploy network infrastructure at the edge. They excel in distributed, remote or harsh environments and can be deployed in offices, operational sites, remote locations, government buildings, financial branches and industrial facilities.

Growth in the adoption of micro data centres is also being driven by their ability to address the evolving challenges of modern IT management. Their purpose is not simply to house technology but to create a secure physical layer for effective cybersecurity and disaster recovery strategies – therefore keeping essential IT systems operational.

### Let's get physical

Cybersecurity is commonly associated with technologies such as firewalls, threat detection, encryption and access management. However, these measures rely on any underlying physical IT infrastructure remaining secure and operational. If servers are damaged, power is interrupted, equipment overheats or a facility becomes inaccessible, even the most advanced cyber defences cannot ensure service availability. For this reason, physical resilience is a critical component of a comprehensive cybersecurity strategy.

The importance of physical resilience is highlighted by the financial impact of cyber incidents. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 estimates that the global average cost of a data breach is $4.44m. Micro data centres help reduce this risk by combining physical security, environmental protection and infrastructure resilience in a single solution. As well as safeguarding critical IT systems against cyberattacks, they also protect against a wide range of other threats including vandalism, accidental damage, equipment failure and environmental hazards, helping organisations maintain business continuity and minimise downtime.

### Road to recovery

Alongside cybersecurity, another advantage of micro data centres is their role in disaster recovery planning. Traditional disaster recovery strategies often depend on large secondary data centres that can be very expensive to build and difficult to locate. Micro data centres provide organisations with greater choice because they can be deployed in a wide range of environments. They can be positioned away from primary facilities, creating physical separation that reduces the risk of a single incident affecting both operational and recovery infrastructure.

Geographical diversity is an important element of resilience. If a primary site and recovery site are located too close together, they may both be affected by the same event, such as flooding, fire, power failure or regional disruption. Micro data centres enable organisations to establish recovery locations that are physically separate while still providing secure and reliable access to essential systems. This approach supports modern disaster recovery strategies that prioritise rapid restoration and operational continuity.

The Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA) region faces a range of infrastructure challenges that make this distributed approach increasingly relevant. The European Environment Agency has highlighted the growing risks associated with climate related events, including extreme weather and flooding, which can affect critical infrastructure. Micro data centres help address these challenges by providing adaptable infrastructure that can be deployed where it is needed most.

### Rules and regulations

For financial institutions, this approach supports regulatory expectations around operational resilience. Banks and insurers must demonstrate that critical services can withstand disruption and recover within acceptable timeframes. Distributed infrastructure using micro data centres provides an additional layer of protection by reducing dependence on a single physical location.

Insurance companies also depend heavily on continuous access to data and digital platforms. Claims processing, customer services, risk analysis and policy management all rely on available IT systems. Any service disruption, no matter how small, can delay services for customers during already challenging situations. Micro data centres help insurers maintain local processing capability and provide additional recovery options when central systems are down.

The public sector faces similar challenges. Local and regional governments increasingly utilise digital platforms for taxation, healthcare administration, public safety, transport and a whole range of public services. The expectation is that these systems should remain available regardless of unexpected events. Micro data centres provide a practical method of strengthening digital infrastructure across multiple locations and enable organisations to design recovery strategies based on risk rather than convenience.

### Features and benefits

When selecting a micro data centre, a range of factors must be considered to ensure the infrastructure meets both current and future requirements. Getting this right first time helps create a resilient, scalable solution that delivers long-term value and reduces the risk of costly upgrades or premature replacement.

Physical security is one of the most important considerations. Secure cabinets, reinforced enclosures, access control mechanisms and monitoring capabilities prevent unauthorised access. For banks and insurance organisations managing sensitive customer data, this protects critical systems from tampering, theft or accidental interference. Government departments and public sector organisations also benefit from this capability. A local authority, emergency service provider or government agency may need secure computing infrastructure in regional offices, operational facilities or remote locations.

Another important feature is integrated fire detection and suppression. Fire remains one of the most significant physical threats to IT infrastructure and conventional fire protection systems are not always sufficient for protecting sensitive electronic equipment. Micro data centres can incorporate dedicated fire detection technologies that identify threats quickly and fire suppression systems minimise damage while protecting equipment and personnel.

### Support structure

Infrastructure resilience is further enhanced through advanced power continuity systems. Power resilience is particularly important across EMEA, where data centre capacity is expanding rapidly but constraints around power, land and grid availability are influencing where organisations deploy infrastructure.

Micro data centres incorporate the latest uninterruptible power supply (UPS) technology, which provides immediate protection against power interruptions. A UPS ensures critical IT equipment remains operational while allowing sufficient time for controlled shutdown procedures or for back-up power systems, such as generators, to take over during prolonged disruptions. In addition, cutting edge power distribution units (PDUs) enable real-time power monitoring, remote management and load balancing, helping to optimise energy usage, prevent circuit overloads and improve overall resilience.

Remote management and monitoring further enhance the value of micro data centres. Pre-installed sensors and software provide centralised oversight, with visibility down to individual outlets. This allows administrators to track temperature, humidity, power usage, security alerts and equipment performance without needing personnel on-site.

Standardisation also delivers significant benefits for those managing decentralised infrastructure assets. Adopting standard off the shelf components enables faster identification and resolution of defects or operational issues. This ensures assets can be restored to full functionality quickly, thereby minimising downtime.

### More than meets the eye

A micro data centre should be viewed as more than a compact IT enclosure. It is a strategic resilience platform that combines physical protection, infrastructure availability and disaster recovery capability. By securing the physical foundation that supports cybersecurity, organisations can improve their ability to withstand attacks, recover from failures and continue delivering essential services.

stories.content:
The data centre developer is in talks to sell AI computing power to the Claude maker

\[SAN FRANCISCO\] Nscale is in talks to sell artificial intelligence computing power to Claude maker Anthropic in a new deal that could be worth about US$45 billion, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters on Monday (Oct 19).

The data centre developer is seeking another major deal with the AI lab for a second facility at its Monarch data centre campus in West Virginia, the person said.

In August, Anthropic struck a deal to spend US$45 billion to rent AI cloud computing power from Nscale’s West Virginia data centre campus. A second Monarch building would deliver 460 megawatts of computing power using Nvidia’s advanced Vera Rubin AI chips, according to the source.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Anthropic also has the right of first refusal on Monarch’s expected third building, the person said, adding discussions were ongoing and details of the plan could change.

Bloomberg, which first reported the news, also said a cohort of investors had urged Anthropic to lower its initial public offering valuation target after a series of market setbacks for AI companies.

Investors have sharpened scrutiny of companies that are increasingly turning to debt-driven AI infrastructure expansion. Last week, Nscale rival CoreWeave’s shares slumped amid concerns over its US$50 billion debt load, fuelling a global sell-off in AI stocks.

The news of a potential tie-up comes after Microsoft pulled out of a deal to anchor a flagship data centre for Nscale following power connection delays that pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s.

Nscale has grown rapidly since launch, increasing its total contracted value from US$100 million to more than US$103 billion in two-and-a-half years and competing with Nebius , Crusoe and Lambda.

According to the Nscale prospectus, Microsoft and Anthropic are expected to be the company’s major customers in the future. REUTERS

stories.title: CMTG cuts CPU use 70% with Lenovo AMD server refresh
stories.summary: The private cloud refresh gave Australian business customers faster SQL reporting and more headroom for AI workloads without disrupting service.
stories.title_zh: CMTG通过Lenovo AMD服务器更新将CPU使用率降低70%
stories.content:
Tue, 20th Oct 2026 (Today)
CMTG has upgraded its private cloud platform with Lenovo ThinkSystem SR675 V3 servers using AMD EPYC 9475F processors, a move it says cut CPU utilisation by 70%.

The infrastructure refresh also reduced RAM usage by 10%, while customers reported faster application performance, including SQL reports running up to three times faster.

The Perth-based managed service provider, which offers private cloud, virtual desktop infrastructure, data storage and application hosting services to Australian small and medium-sized businesses, replaced server hardware nearing the end of its service life. It aimed to improve customer experience and create room for more demanding workloads, including artificial intelligence applications.

The updated platform remains based on Lenovo servers with VMware and Citrix virtualisation layers. CMTG said the new configuration improved virtual desktop performance while lowering the compute resources needed to support them.

For customers using computer-aided design applications through the company's virtual desktop infrastructure, the faster processor clock speeds improved responsiveness, even on endpoint devices not usually suited to graphics-heavy tasks. In Citrix Windows 11 VDI benchmarks, CMTG achieved 60 frames per second, which it described as the platform limit.

Management said the switchover was completed overnight without disrupting customers. CMTG used Lenovo XClarity Pro software to automate parts of the deployment and migration.

"Moving to Lenovo ThinkSystem SR675 V3 servers powered by AMD EPYC processors is night and day as far as performance is concerned, both for us and our customers," said Carl Filpo, Managing Director, CMTG. "By upgrading our infrastructure, we can provision virtual desktops with superior end-user experience and at lower cost, improving customer retention and growth."

CMTG said the upgrade comes as cloud and managed service providers face pressure to support larger and more varied workloads without expanding infrastructure at the same rate. It has also been competing with Microsoft Azure Virtual Desktop and was looking for a way to strengthen its private cloud offering.

### Customer response

Customers noticed the difference quickly after the new servers went live, with users reporting faster performance across applications, particularly in SQL-based reporting workloads.

"Moving to Lenovo ThinkSystem SR675 V3 servers powered by AMD EPYC processors is night and day as far as performance is concerned, both for us and our customers," said Filpo. "The morning after we completed the switch over, we had customers calling us to ask: 'what did you do? Our applications are so fast!' with one customer saying that one particular report has gone from taking several minutes to a few seconds."

CMTG also said the lower CPU load has created additional headroom in its environment. Nick Hughes, Technical Sales Manager at CMTG, said the business saw no performance impact even with 2:1 contention while the environment was being stood up.

### AI planning

CMTG said the refreshed platform provides a foundation for AI-related services customers may want to run in a locally hosted environment. It sees demand for secure, Australia-based infrastructure that can support AI workloads while remaining under managed control.

AMD linked the deployment to a broader shift in infrastructure planning as more organisations move from testing AI tools to using them in production systems.

"As enterprises bring AI into production, the conversation is shifting from simply adding more compute to building infrastructure that delivers the right balance of performance, efficiency and operational control," said Alexey Navolokin, General Manager, Sales, APAC, AMD. "CMTG's deployment of AMD EPYC Server CPUs illustrates that the same infrastructure investments improving virtual desktop performance today can also provide the compute foundation needed for future AI services."

CMTG said it reviewed several processor vendors during the refresh and chose AMD after examining market options and receiving a reference from Citrix, which it said uses AMD in its own platform. It also cited its long-standing relationship with Lenovo and past experience with the vendor's hardware and support services.

Founded in 1998, CMTG is headquartered in Perth and focuses on managed private cloud systems, backups, virtual machines and hosted applications for business customers across Australia.

stories.title: Top hyperscalers likely to have more AI-linked debt than now known, S&P Global warns
stories.summary: S&P Global has warned that top hyperscalers likely carry more AI-related debt than is publicly visible, pointing to financing structures that keep obligations off balance sheets. The rating agency flags potential transparency gaps as AI infrastructure spending accelerates.
stories.why_it_matters: Hidden leverage raises credit-risk questions for investors and lenders exposed to AI infrastructure, and could prompt rating pressure or disclosure scrutiny if spending outpaces cash flows.
stories.title_zh: S&P Global警告：头部hyperscaler的AI相关债务可能超出已知规模
stories.summary_zh: 标普全球（S&P Global）警告称，头部 hyperscaler 实际承担的 AI 相关债务可能高于公开披露的水平，指出存在将义务置于表外的融资结构。随着 AI 基础设施支出加速，该评级机构提示了潜在的透明度缺口。
stories.why_zh: 隐性杠杆为涉足 AI 基础设施的投资者与贷款方带来信用风险疑问，若支出超过现金流，还可能引发评级压力或披露审查。
stories.content:
S&P Global estimates the world's biggest tech firms are likely to have more AI-linked liabilities than currently known, although its top analyst for the sector sees no need to change any ratings at present.

Debt issued by AI infrastructure providers and so-called 'neocloud' firms such as Nvidia-backed CoreWeave has sunk to increasingly stressed levels in recent weeks amid concerns about the aggressive scale of their borrowing.

S&P's Global Head for Digital Infrastructure Mark Habib said the biggest risk to hyperscalers' ratings remained whether expected profits fail to materialise.

But he also highlighted so-called 'interconnected financing structures', where hyperscalers effectively guarantee huge data centre builds, or smaller AI companies.

"It is safe to assume that there is more (debt) out there that we are not seeing," Habib said during a roundtable in London.

"If it's not reported, then it's not part of the disclosure by the hyperscalers. Also, if we are not rating the transactions where this liability may accrue, then the fact of the matter is that we might not have the visibility."

S&P expects the top six US hyperscalers — Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Oracle, Meta, and SpaceX — to spend more than US$7 trillion ($10 trillion) on data centres and other AI-related capex between 2025 and 2030, and have negative free cash flow until at least next year.

Habib said there wasn't an estimate of how much additional debt the circular financing might add to firms' balance sheets, although he said S&P was trying to take a "holistic" view overall.

Back in July, it downgraded Oracle to BBB-, the lowest rung of 'investment grade', on concerns about its AI spending and what it called "an uncertain path to profitability".

Habib was also asked whether the recent market selloff of bonds linked to the aggressive AI buildout was a sign that investors see them as riskier than ratings indicate.

"For now, we don't have the view that there is a major disconnect that needs to force our ratings to change at this point," he said, saying S&P's scores were designed to take a longer-term view.

He said what could change that view was if it became clear the amount of money being spent was no longer sustainable.

"And that could come from a variety of drivers," Habib said. "Further increases in the investments (by AI firms), or a view that the revenue rate of competition is getting too intense."

stories.title: 'Sky glow': Data centres could threaten Mackenzie's dark sky status
stories.summary: Residents fear fast-track data centres could flood Twizel with light pollution, putting Mackenzie's dark sky reserve status and tourism at risk.
stories.title_zh: “天空辉光”：数据中心或威胁新西兰Mackenzie暗夜保护区地位
stories.content:
Fears are mounting the Mackenzie could become home to large-scale data centres, with one expert warning the district's dark sky reserve status was at risk.

Twizel residents demanded action from the Mackenzie District Council after raising concerns about data centres, fast-track consenting, and the Government's new Natural Environment Act and Planning Bill at a public forum earlier this month.

Twizel Community Board member Zoe White warned the new laws, which replace the Resource Management Act, allowed ministers to set aside environmental limits without consulting affected communities – if they deemed the public benefit outweighed local harm and the "needs and aspirations of the community".

White pointed to the Datagrid project near Invercargill, where resource consent was not notified after the Southland District Council deemed the environmental impacts were "less than minor".

Stargazing guide and NASA astronomer Daniel Gaussen told councillors data centres created light pollution, utilising LED lighting and operating around the clock.

"Our atmosphere is very good at scattering blue light, which means basically what we're going to see if we have a big data centre in Twizel is a huge sky glow."

He warned the sky glow could destroy the Aoraki/Mackenzie International Dark Sky Reserve's gold-standard status and impact his astronomical research for NASA.

"It's a big selling point for this region, it can be lost. If we continue to increase light pollution, … we will reach a sky glow limit which if we pass it, we lose the dark sky reserve status."

Mt Cook Lakeside Retreat owner Kaye Paardekooper said the district was facing a "perfect storm" for non-notified development.

"You've got the data centre push, the resource management reform, you've got the local government reform," Paardekooper said.

"You've got fast-track, and I believe it's coming as a perfect storm."

As one of 28 New Zealand accommodation providers to receive a Michelin Key, Paardekooper said industrial developments would put employment, tourism, and that status at risk.

"It's not just vacant land waiting to be developed. It's open space, it's natural, quiet, its dark skies, its mountain and lake views … Mackenzie feels different because of what's not here."

She said the Mackenzie's location within a basin meant the effects of industrial development would be felt across the district.

"It's like a big reverberating, echoing basin."

Geospatial analyst Jana Kaeppler raised concerns about potential noise caused by data centres, saying the question was not simply how loud they were, but how the noise would affect the district.

"Twizel is very different from the city or an established industrial area, we have a very quiet night time environment and weather conditions can affect how sound travels."

Large data centres produced noise from cooling systems, transformers, backup generators and equipment handling, along with periods of low-frequency sound, Kaeppler said.

Accommodation providers, tourism, and resident satisfaction would be impacted, Kaeppler said as she called for enforceable site monitoring of any future development.

Twizel fishing guides Brad Snow and Ben Booth addressed councillors together, warning that data centres produced overflow that would impact the district's fishing and recreation.

"The overflow goes into the canal or the lake," Snow said.

"Fish will start dying as soon as that water starts going over 18 degrees."

Data centres used between 600,000 and one million litres of water a day, he said, which would create huge impacts on water levels over summer.

But that was just the start, he said, with chemicals, anti-scaling agents and chlorine used by data centres entering waterways, such as Benmore where families had gathered for decades.

"If this goes ahead you can say goodbye to a lot of that, and the both of us would probably leave … We're not going to be having people paying us to take them out to water I'm too scared to put my kids in."

Snow said their businesses contributed about $500,000 annually to the local economy, something that would be lost if data centres were built.

General manager of Inflite Tourism at Pukaki Airport, Gemma Parton, urged councillors to consider the visual impact of developments on tourism operations, saying it was important to remember why people came to the district.

"Visitors come here for the vast number of unique experiences we offer ... They're not just paying for a skydive, they're actually paying for a memory. When people jump out they cherish the memory."

Mackenzie District mayor Scott Aronsen acknowledged the concerns, saying while recent legislation restricted council interference, he was in regular contact with the Waitaki District Council and Government officials who were "looking at some changes".

Closing the public forum, Aronsen told Twizel Community Board chair Mary Murdoch she would need to lobby the Government directly over the community's concerns.

"You guys are going to have to do some lobbying … we'll do as much as we can but at the end of the day, they'll listen to people on the ground."

Murdoch had worked to educate the community on potential industrial developments in the district, forming a Twizel working group and holding a meeting in August to educate residents.

At the time, several applications for solar projects in the Mackenzie were progressing through fast-track, with the Haldon Station Solar Farm receiving approval in August.

Other projects included the Twizel Solar Project, which received resource consent in August, the Balmoral Station Solar Array and the Grampians Solar Project.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop said the reforms aimed to make consenting faster, simpler, and more predictable, with fewer applications requiring public notification.

"This means communities can help shape the bigger decisions about growth and development, without unnecessarily revisiting those decisions through every individual consent application."

Bishop said where a consent application is not publicly notified, the legislation provides mechanisms to review notification decisions through the Planning Tribunal.

He said the Natural Environment Act provided the Minister flexibility to enable activity through national standards, considering the cost and benefits, potential human and environmental harm, implications, and mitigating conditions.

"The new system establishes enforceable environmental limits to protect human health and ecosystems ... This ensures decisions can account for wider public benefits while maintaining appropriate environmental protections," Bishop said.

However, Bishop said that neither the bill or act contained specific provisions protecting dark skies.

While councils would continue to manage light spill through local plans, Bishop said, reserve protections would require a council justification report subject to public submissions, appeals, and set standards.

stories.title: China AI Data Centre Boom Faces ROI Test
stories.summary: A Goldman Sachs report finds China's AI data centre sector under growing pressure to demonstrate profitable returns as financing costs climb. The industry's focus is shifting away from rapid capacity buildout toward capital efficiency and strategies to improve investment returns.
stories.why_it_matters: A pivot from expansion to returns discipline could slow new project approvals and reshape financing terms, affecting developers, lenders, and local governments that have counted on data centre construction as a growth engine.
stories.title_zh: 中国AI数据中心热潮面临投资回报考验
stories.summary_zh: 高盛（Goldman Sachs）报告显示，随着融资成本上升，中国 AI 数据中心行业正面临越来越大的投资回报证明压力。行业重心正从快速扩张产能转向资本效率及提升回报率的策略。
stories.why_zh: 从扩张转向回报纪律可能放缓新项目审批并重塑融资条件，影响那些将数据中心建设视为增长引擎的开发商、贷款方及地方政府。
stories.content:
China's rapidly expanding artificial intelligence (AI) data centre sector faces growing pressure to demonstrate profitable returns on investment.This is due to rising financing costs and investor concerns, shifting attention from capacity expansion to capital efficiency, a Goldman Sachs research report said.Stronger-than-expected demand for AI infrastructure has improved the medium-term growth outlook for Chinese data centre operators, the report noted. However, as new orders translate into long-term contracted capacity, the sector is increasingly being judged on its ability to generate returns that exceed the cost of capital.Goldman Sachs examined three business models in China's data centre sector. These include traditional powered-shell facilities, integrated AI data centres that provide graphics processing unit (GPU) computing services under long-term contracts, and AI token factories that generate revenue by processing AI workloads.Traditional powered-shell data centres offer relatively stable infrastructure revenues but may generate limited returns without favourable financing or asset-sale opportunities. The report estimated gross return on invested capital (ROIC) at around 5 per cent under its base-case assumptions.Integrated AI data centres could generate higher returns by providing GPU-as-a-service under three-to-five-year contracts. Profitability depends on GPU procurement costs, rental prices, financing and the risk of hardware becoming obsolete. Goldman Sachs estimated that certain configurations involving Nvidia B300-equivalent servers could support a 15 per cent annual ROIC under specific pricing and capital-cost assumptions.AI token factories could offer still higher returns by monetising computing capacity through AI inference and token production. The report modelled an ROIC of around 21 per cent for an asset-light token factory and around 43 per cent for one owning its GPU infrastructure. These are model-based estimates, not actual returns achieved by companies.The report also highlighted potential opportunities for operators to improve capital efficiency through asset recycling, lower-cost debt and overseas expansion. Goldman Sachs' analysis suggests that investment returns, financing costs and the ability to monetise computing capacity will become increasingly important.

stories.title: Optical PCIe Extends AI Rack Design Flexibility
stories.summary: A demonstration by Lumentum, Astera Labs, and Corning shows how optical PCIe could offer more flexible rack designs for AI data centers. This approach aims to relax constraints on reach, signal integrity, power, thermal management, and cable density.
stories.title_zh: Optical PCIe为AI机架设计带来更大灵活性
stories.content:
Optical Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) is emerging as a method to ease some pressures in AI rack designs, according to a demonstration by Lumentum, Astera Labs, and Corning. Traditional electrical interconnects face limitations in reach, signal integrity, power, thermal management, and cable density as AI racks become denser and PCIe data rates increase.The companies presented a rack-level demonstration at the 2026 OCP Global Summit in San Jose. The setup combined Astera Labs' Scorpio Smart Fabric Switch, Lumentum's optical interconnect, and Corning multimode fiber. These links used vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers (VCSELs). Lumentum described the system as a proof of concept, not a product announcement.Christian Urricariet, senior director of product and strategic marketing at Lumentum, noted that optical PCIe can relax several system constraints. It moves data over lightweight, low-loss optical links across longer distances. Joshua Fennimore, commercial technology manager at Corning Optical Communications, stated that optical connections can span tens to hundreds of meters within a data center. This compares to passive copper connections, which are generally limited to a few meters.Higher PCIe data rates make electrical links more sensitive to loss, crosstalk, and equalization requirements, Urricariet said. Designers may need to add retimers or place connected devices closer together. High-speed copper cables can also become bulky and difficult to route and manage.
### Reshaping Rack and Row Design

Fiber gives designers more room to separate systems while maintaining high-speed connectivity, Fennimore explained. This allows systems to be separated across racks or rows inside a data center. Operators gain greater flexibility to optimise rack layouts around compute density, power, cooling, serviceability, and cable management.Jignesh Shah, senior director of product marketing for the Signal Connectivity Group at Astera Labs, indicated that optical PCIe could enable scale-up designs across multiple racks. This includes disaggregated architectures with dedicated racks for GPUs, switches, and memory. Optical PCIe also enables high-density solutions required for high-radix switches and GPU applications.Urricariet added that optical PCIe could make it easier to build more modular and composable rack-scale designs. This is particularly relevant in AI environments where power delivery, thermal limits, and serviceability are critical.
### Copper's Continued Role

Copper remains the more established and cost-effective choice for short distances, according to Shah. He noted that once designs exceed about 3 meters of reach, evaluating both copper and optical options becomes sensible. Shah stated that copper currently offers the best total cost of ownership (TCO) for anything within a few meters due to its maturity.Urricariet clarified that the goal is not to eliminate copper PCIe connections. Instead, it is to expand the practical system architectures as AI racks grow in scale and complexity. Moving from a demonstration to broad deployment requires further work across system integration, reliability, manufacturing, and customer qualification.

stories.summary: AI chip startup Tenstorrent has raised US$1.5 billion at a US$6.2 billion valuation. The fresh capital will support continued development of the company's Galaxy server line as it competes in the market for alternatives to dominant GPU platforms.
stories.why_it_matters: The raise signals investors still see room for challengers to incumbent AI silicon, and fresh funding for alternative architectures could broaden hardware options for data centre operators wary of supply concentration.

stories.summary_zh: AI 芯片初创公司 Tenstorrent 以 62 亿美元估值完成 15 亿美元融资。新资金将支持其 Galaxy 服务器产品线的持续开发，以在主流 GPU 平台替代品市场中展开竞争。
stories.why_zh: 此轮融资表明投资者仍认为挑战现有 AI 芯片厂商存在空间，替代架构获得的新资金可为担忧供应集中的数据中心运营商拓宽硬件选择。
stories.content:
AI chip startup Tenstorrent has raised $1.5 billion in a Series E round, valuing the company at $6.2bn.

The round, which more than doubles the company’s previous valuation, was led by Trace Capital and Innovation X, with participation from ARK Invest, Cadence Ventures, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Maverick Silicon, Morgan Stanley, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price, among others.

In a statement, Tenstorrent said it would use the funding to scale manufacturing and introduce new generations of its Galaxy servers, whilst also increasing its global workforce.

The servers, which began shipping in April of this year, comprise 32 of the company’s RISC-V Blackhole processors with Tensix AI cores, offering 23 petaflops of FP8 compute performance.

“We built one architecture and sell it at every size,” said Jim Keller, CEO of Tenstorrent. “The future of compute is open, scalable, and owned by the people building on it. Our investors believe in that model too, and we appreciate their support.”

Founded in 2016, Tenstorrent builds scalable artificial intelligence accelerators for both the cloud and Edge in order to compete with Nvidia’s GPUs. The company is also developing a RISC-V CPU and licenses its designs to other organizations.

In October 2022, Tenstorrent founder Ljubisa Bajic job-swapped with Keller, the company’s then CTO, before stepping down from the company entirely in March of the following year to found Taalas, a separate AI chip startup.

Tenstorrent completed a Series D funding round in December 2024, which saw the company valued at more than $2.6 billion. Raising $693 million, investors included Jeff Bezos' Bezos Expeditions, Samsung Securities, and AFW Partners.

In June 2026, it was reported that Qualcomm was exploring an acquisition of the chip startup.

stories.title: Data Vault lines up 11 partners for new Auckland data centre
stories.summary: New Zealand-owned data centre operator Data Vault plans to build a 3MW facility on Auckland’s North Shore, with 11 connectivity and service partners confirmed ahead of its planned opening in the second half of 2027. The development forms part of a wider expansion programme targeting approximately 6MW of additional capacity across Auckland, Hamilton and Wellington […]
stories.title_zh: Data Vault为奥克兰新数据中心敲定11家合作伙伴
stories.content:
New Zealand-owned data centre operator Data Vault plans to build a 3MW facility on Auckland’s North Shore, with 11 connectivity and service partners confirmed ahead of its planned opening in the second half of 2027.

The development forms part of a wider expansion programme targeting approximately 6MW of additional capacity across Auckland, Hamilton and Wellington over the coming years. Data Vault said the building for the North Shore facility has already been acquired, with fitout scheduled to begin in 2027 and capacity to be brought online in stages as customer demand grows.

The company has identified 5.3MW of additional capacity across four projects: the new North Shore facility, a further 1MW at its existing Grafton data centre in Auckland, another 1MW at its Te Rapa facility in Hamilton, and approximately 300kW in Wellington. Further opportunities are under consideration to meet its broader 6MW expansion target.

The announcement follows continued growth at Grafton, where Data Vault said Data Hall 3 is fully contracted. Data Hall 4, backed by an international anchor tenant, is scheduled to become operational in the first quarter of 2027, followed by Data Hall 5 in the third quarter.

“We’ve seen significant demand from network operators, cloud providers and international technology companies looking for high-quality colocation in New Zealand,” said Peter White, general manager at Data Vault. “The North Shore development is the next logical step. We’ve secured the building and expect to start bringing capacity online next year, giving our customers another Auckland location and greater geographic diversity.”

Data Vault has operated in New Zealand since 2004, with facilities in Auckland and Hamilton. It expanded into Wellington through an operations and management agreement with service provider Vital, announced in 2025, extending its reach across the country’s three major data centre markets. The arrangement was intended to bring the Wellington facility into Data Vault’s operations, with modernisation planned to align it with the company’s existing standards.

### Connectivity partners lined up for launch

The North Shore facility will open with 11 confirmed connectivity and service partners: Eon Fibre, Devoli, EdgeIX, Verge Infrastructure, WaveSquared, Hostpearl, Vetta Group, Mercury, Purelink, Vital and Megaport. Data Vault expects to announce additional partners before the facility opens.

The partners will provide access to fibre networks, internet services, internet exchanges, cloud connectivity and other network solutions. The operator said it would maintain a carrier-neutral model, allowing customers to choose their preferred providers.

“We’re not building a facility and then hoping the network providers turn up,” White said. “We’ve already confirmed 11 launch partners, with more to come. Customers will have access to a wide range of services and providers from day one.”

Data Vault said its Grafton facility is approaching 70 autonomous system numbers (ASNs) across its network ecosystem, with access to internet exchanges including EdgeIX, NZIX and MegaIX.

Connectivity is a central part of the company’s positioning. Its existing Auckland facility offers access to more than 50 network providers, according to its website, alongside carrier-neutral colocation and connections to major network and peering services.

### Efficiency and mid-density colocation

Data Vault said energy efficiency would be a focus across its expansion programme, with modern cooling systems, aisle containment and efficient power infrastructure intended to increase the proportion of available power that can be used by customer IT equipment.

The company already operates rooftop solar installations at its Grafton and Hamilton facilities and plans further installations, including at North Shore. Its website reports a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.14 for its existing operations. The company has not provided a target PUE for the new facility.

“Power efficiency is becoming increasingly important for our customers,” White said. “We’re investing in modern cooling technology and better facility design to maximise the amount of power available for customer IT equipment.”

While much of the data centre market’s attention is on hyperscale and AI infrastructure, Data Vault said it sees demand for mid-density colocation from network operators, cloud providers, managed service providers and enterprises. “There’s a significant market for reliable, well-connected mid-density rack space, and that’s where we see a real opportunity,” White said.

“We want to provide flexible infrastructure that works for customers of all sizes, whether they need a single rack or a larger dedicated environment.”

The operator said it was also nearing completion of a SOC 2 readiness programme, with enhanced physical security, monitoring, operational procedures and governance controls planned for rollout across its facilities alongside the North Shore development. The programme is intended to support progression towards independent SOC 2 attestation.

Data Vault said it would continue to focus on carrier-neutral connectivity, energy efficiency and flexible colocation as it expands its footprint. “We’re not trying to be the biggest data centre operator in New Zealand,” White said. “Our focus is on building highly connected, efficient and reliable facilities, providing good service and making sure we have capacity available as our customers grow.”
